title: Short Stuff: Greenbrier Bunker
summary: Short Stuff episode on the Greenbrier Bunker, a secret Cold War fallout shelter built beneath the Greenbrier resort in White Sulphur Springs, West Virginia, to house the U.S. Congress during a nuclear attack. Covers the choice of the resort as cover, the project's construction in the early 1960s (code-named Project Greek Island, roughly $14 million, completed in 1962 before the Cuban missile crisis), its depth and size, the decontamination and dormitory facilities, meeting rooms for the House, Senate and joint sessions, the jail and riot gear, and how journalist Ted Gup's 1992 article exposed it and led to it being decommissioned and opened for public tours. Also mentions the Supreme Court's planned relocation and staff and family questions.

segments.title: Introduction to the Greenbrier bunker
segments.summary: Josh introduces the topic: a secret Cold War bunker hidden beneath a resort hotel built to keep Congress functioning after a nuclear attack. He mentions the Greenbrier's location and Dorothy Draper's redesign, and how the bunker was kept secret until a reporter exposed it.

segments.title: Exposure and decommissioning
segments.summary: The hosts describe Ted Gup's article that revealed the bunker, after which it became useless and was decommissioned within three years, with public tours given. The bunk beds were assigned to members of Congress for about thirty years.

segments.title: Cover story and construction details
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the Forsyth Associates cover story for the TV technicians who maintained the bunker, the code name Project Greek Island, the location's proximity to Washington, D.C., and the construction at about $14 million, completed in 1962 just before the Cuban missile crisis. Its depth is about 720 feet and it spans roughly 112,000 square feet over two levels.

segments.title: Facilities inside the bunker
segments.summary: The hosts describe the bunker's facilities: decontamination rooms, dormitories with sixty beds in each of eighteen rooms, a cafeteria and kitchen, a broadcast media room, three meeting rooms for the House, Senate and joint sessions, a pharmacy, and a small jail with riot gear and straitjackets. Public areas of the resort were also sealed off in an emergency.

segments.title: Access, Supreme Court plans, and staff questions
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the bunker's entrance behind a high voltage door, the planned relocation of the Supreme Court to a Greenbrier grove park, the train route from D.C., and whether congressional staff and families would be brought along.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck thank each other and credit the Atomic Heritage Foundation and NPR as sources, then close the short episode.
